```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
```

## A small tibble to practise on

```{r}
#| label: toy
sales <- tibble(
  act_use_cat = c("S/F Res", "S/F Res", "S/F Res",
                  "Strata Res", "Strata Res", "Strata Res"),
  sale_year = c(2024, 2025, 2025, 2024, 2024, 2025),
  price = c(1800000, 2000000, 5000000, 600000, 700000, 800000)
)
sales
```

## summarise() turns many rows into one

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: sales-summarise
sales
```
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: summarise
sales |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price),
            n = n())
```

`n()` counts the rows.
:::
::::

Other summary functions: `sum()`, `median()`, `min()`, and `max()`.

## group_by() only adds a label

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: sales-label
sales
```
:::

::: {.column .small width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: group-label
by_type <- sales |> group_by(act_use_cat)
by_type
```
:::
::::

Same rows, same values. The new `# Groups` line records which column defines the groups.

## summarise() reads the label

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: by-type
by_type
```
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: group
by_type |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price),
            n = n())
```

`summarise()` runs once per group. `mean()` gets one type's prices at a time.
:::
::::

::: {.key-point}
Two steps, two jobs: `group_by()` adds the label, and the verb after it, such as `summarise()`, `mutate()`, or `filter()`, works within each group.
:::

## filter() reads the label too

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: by-type-filter
by_type
```
:::

::: {.column .small width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: filter-grouped
by_type |> filter(price == max(price))
sales |> filter(price == max(price))
```
:::
::::

With the label, `max(price)` is each type's highest price. Without it, it is the highest of all six sales.

::: {.notes}
- If students ask whether every verb reads the label: `arrange()` does not. It sorts the whole table unless you add `.by_group = TRUE`, which sorts by the grouping column first. `by_type |> arrange(desc(sale_year))` mixes the two types; `arrange(desc(sale_year), .by_group = TRUE)` keeps them together.
- For `lag()` this makes no difference: a whole-table sort by year already puts each group's rows in year order. Only the printed order changes, as on the "sort order" answer slide of the growth practice.
:::

## Predict the output

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: sales-predict
sales
```
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: predict-code
#| eval: false
sales |>
  filter(price > 1000000) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: predict-out
#| echo: false
sales |>
  filter(price > 1000000) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

No strata sale is above $1 million, so `Strata Res` is missing, not 0.
:::
:::
::::

## summarise() removes one level of grouping

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: sales-groups
sales
```
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: groups
by_type_year <- sales |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year) |>
  summarise(n = n())
group_vars(by_type_year)
```
:::
::::

The result is still grouped by `act_use_cat`. Later steps then work within each type, which may not be what you want.

::: {.key-point}
Add `.groups = "drop"` to `summarise()`, or call `ungroup()`, when you are done with groups.
:::

## mutate() reads the label too, and keeps every row

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="30%"}
```{r}
#| label: tb
tb <- tibble(
  a = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2),
  b = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4)
)
tb
```
:::

::: {.column width="68%"}
```{r}
#| label: group-mutate
tb |>
  group_by(a) |>
  mutate(group_total = sum(b),
         share_of_group = b / sum(b)) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::
::::

A summary function such as `sum()` gives one value per group, repeated on every row.

## lag() looks at the previous row

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .small width="30%"}
```{r}
#| label: tb-lag
tb
```
:::

::: {.column width="68%"}
```{r}
#| label: lag
tb |>
  group_by(a) |>
  mutate(previous = lag(b), change = b - lag(b)) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::
::::

## Application: average prices by year

```{r}
#| label: avg-price
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")

avg_price <- bca |>
  mutate(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

avg_price |> head(3)
```

## Check the last date before you compare years

```{r}
#| label: partial-year
bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) >= 2024) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(sales = n(), first_sale = min(sale_date), last_sale = max(sale_date))
```

::: {.warning}
The file ends on `r paste(mday(max(bca$sale_date)), format(max(bca$sale_date), "%B %Y"))`. On a chart by year, 2026 looks like a collapse in sales, and its average covers only winter sales. Drop incomplete years, or compare the same months in each year.
:::

## An average can fall while every type rises

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: mix-shift
bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% 2016:2017) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(all = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
            sf = mean(price[act_use_cat == "S/F Res"], na.rm = TRUE),
            strata = mean(price[act_use_cat == "Strata Res"], na.rm = TRUE),
            sf_share = mean(act_use_cat == "S/F Res"))
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: mix-shift-numbers
#| include: false
mix <- bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% 2016:2017) |>
  group_by(sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(sf_share = mean(act_use_cat == "S/F Res"))
```

::: {.key-point}
Both types rose in 2017, yet the average fell, because single-family homes dropped from `r round(100 * mix$sf_share[1])`% to `r round(100 * mix$sf_share[2])`% of sales. An average price describes the mix of homes sold. Compare within types, or use a regression (deck 17).
:::

## Practice (AI on): a price index

Using `avg_price`, compute a price index for each `act_use_cat`: each year's average price divided by that type's average price in **2010**.

The index is 1 in 2010. An index of 1.5 means prices 50% above their 2010 level.

Try writing it yourself first, for five minutes. It doesn't have to run.

::: {.notes}
- Time the five minutes. Then everyone moves on to the agent, whether or not their code runs.
- Ask two or three students to show their attempts before anyone runs the agent.
- Look for a missing `group_by()`, which runs without a warning but divides some years by the other type's 2010 price (question 1); `filter(sale_year == 2010)`, which keeps only 2010; and a row position such as `avg_price[11]` (question 2). Leave them; the reading slide catches them.
- An index for each type compares within types, as the previous slide advised.
:::

## Give the task to your agent

::: {.small}
```text
Create scripts/dplyr_2.qmd. From data/bca262.rds, save the average sale
price for each act_use_cat and sale year as avg_price. Then compute a
price index for each act_use_cat: each year's average price divided by
that type's average price in 2010. Save it as price_index.
```
:::

Run the code it writes. Then read it before you go on.

::: {.notes}
- Not yet tested with an agent.
- The student `AGENTS.md` says 2026 is a partial year, and tells the agent to stop and offer options when a choice of years changes the results. If it asks whether to keep 2026, let students choose; question 3 comes back to it.
- The agent may write `.by = act_use_cat` inside `mutate()` instead of `group_by()` and `ungroup()`; it does the same. It may also multiply by 100, so that 2010 is 100.
:::

## Answer

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: index
price_index <- avg_price |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  mutate(index_2010 = avg_price / avg_price[sale_year == 2010]) |>
  ungroup()

price_index |> filter(sale_year %in% c(2010, 2020))
```

## Read the agent's code (AI off)

Compare the agent's code with yours. Where does it differ, and why? Then answer without asking the agent, editing and running the code yourself.

1. Remove the grouping (the `group_by()` line, or `.by =`). Predict: an error, a warning, or a wrong index? Run it. Is the index still 1 in 2010?
2. Another agent took the 2010 price as `avg_price[11]`, because 2010 is the 11th year. Its index matches yours. When would it be wrong?
3. Does the agent's result include 2026? Would you report its index?

::: {.notes}
- Question 1: no error and no warning. Both 2010 rows still show 1, so checking the base year does not catch it. Every other year is wrong: the single-family index for 2011 becomes 2.33 instead of 1.17.
- Question 2 replaces the old "Row positions are fragile" slide.
- Question 3: the strata index rises from 1.94 in 2025 to 2.01 in 2026, but against 1 January to 11 March 2025, strata prices were flat (about $838,000 then, $836,000 now). Single-family prices fell 8% against the same months, not 6%.
:::

## Answer: no grouping

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: index-ungrouped
# 1. No error, no warning, and 2010 is still 1. Without groups,
#    avg_price[sale_year == 2010] is two prices, one per type,
#    and R reuses the pair in turn down all the rows
avg_price |>
  mutate(no_groups = avg_price / avg_price[sale_year == 2010]) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  mutate(with_groups = avg_price / avg_price[sale_year == 2010]) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(sale_year %in% 2010:2011)
```
:::

## Answer: row positions are fragile

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: nth
# 2. Sorted newest first, the 11th year is 2016. A missing or
#    dropped year moves it too. Pick the year by its value
avg_price |>
  arrange(desc(sale_year)) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(year_in_row_11 = sale_year[11])
```

## Answer: 2026 is a partial year

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: index-2026
# 3. The 2026 index compares winter sales with all of 2025.
#    Compare the same months instead: 1 January to 11 March
last_day <- max(bca$sale_date)

bca |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% 2025:2026,
         yday(sale_date) <= yday(last_day)) |>  # yday(): day of the year
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price), .groups = "drop")
```
:::

## Practice (AI on): annual growth

Using `avg_price`, compute the annual growth rate of the average price for each `act_use_cat`: (this year − last year) / last year.

Try writing it yourself first, for five minutes. It doesn't have to run.

::: {.notes}
- Time the five minutes, as before.
- Look for `lag()` without `group_by()`, which changes only one row (question 2), and for no `arrange()`. `avg_price` comes out of `summarise()` sorted by type and year, so it works here, but not after a different sort (question 1).
:::

## Give the task to your agent

::: {.small}
```text
In scripts/dplyr_2.qmd, add the annual growth rate of avg_price for each
act_use_cat: (this year - last year) / last year. Save it as price_growth.
```
:::

Run the code it writes. Then read it before you go on.

::: {.notes}
- Not yet tested with an agent.
- The agent may write `avg_price / lag(avg_price) - 1`, the same formula.
- It may write `lag(avg_price, order_by = sale_year)`, which does not depend on row order. Question 1 then changes nothing, which is worth pointing out.
:::

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: growth
avg_price |>
  arrange(act_use_cat, sale_year) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  mutate(growth = (avg_price - lag(avg_price)) / lag(avg_price)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(sale_year %in% 2023:2025)
```
:::

## Read the agent's code (AI off)

Compare the agent's code with yours. Where does it differ, and why? Then answer without asking the agent, editing and running the code yourself.

1. Add `arrange(desc(sale_year))` right before the line that computes the growth rate. Predict the 2025 growth rates, then run it.
2. Remove the grouping. Which rows change? Would you notice?
3. Compute the 2023 growth rate for single-family homes by hand, from the two prices in `avg_price`. Does it match the agent's?

::: {.notes}
- Question 1: single-family growth in 2025 turns from −3.5% to +6.6%, with no error. Unless the agent used `order_by = sale_year`.
- Question 2: only the first strata year changes, from `NA` to −90%: 2000 strata prices compared with 2026 single-family prices. Hard to notice in a table of recent years.
:::

## Answer: sort order

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: growth-desc
# 1. lag() takes the row above, which is now the next year.
#    Sort by year first, or write lag(avg_price, order_by = sale_year)
avg_price |>
  arrange(desc(sale_year)) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  mutate(growth = (avg_price - lag(avg_price)) / lag(avg_price)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(sale_year %in% 2023:2025)
```
:::

## Answer: lag() without groups

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: growth-ungrouped
# 2. One row changes: strata 2000 is compared with single-family 2026
avg_price |>
  arrange(act_use_cat, sale_year) |>
  mutate(growth = (avg_price - lag(avg_price)) / lag(avg_price)) |>
  filter(sale_year == 2000)
```

## Answer: a check by hand

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: growth-by-hand
# 3. Single-family homes, 2022 and 2023
avg_price |> filter(act_use_cat == "S/F Res", sale_year %in% 2022:2023)
(2004597 - 2059445) / 2059445
```
